ExxonMobil attributes the sharp rise to a **tight refining market**:

- **Demand recovered:** Gasoline and diesel demand returned to pre-pandemic levels, although jet fuel demand remained below historical levels.
- **Refining capacity fell:** Refinery shutdowns and a lack of investment during the pandemic reduced industry capacity. ExxonMobil says more than 3 million barrels per day of capacity had been taken offline.
- **Supply was constrained:** Supply-chain constraints and low inventories added to the tightness as demand recovered.

The filing says refining margins rose well above the top of their 2010–2019 historical range. [ExxonMobil 2022 Form 10-K, pp. 47, 53–54](XOM_2022_10K.pdf)

The filing attributes PCC’s 2021 revenue decline to lower aircraft production. The COVID-19 pandemic materially reduced commercial air travel, prompting airlines to delay or cancel aircraft orders, while the industry also reduced inventories. Both factors depressed demand for PCC’s products. [Form 10-K, p. K-49]

More broadly, Berkshire says the sudden drop in air travel led to reduced aircraft build rates and customer destocking at extraordinary rates. Production delays in Boeing’s 737 MAX and 787 programs also adversely affected PCC’s aerospace business. [Form 10-K, p. K-12]

Apple’s fiscal 2023 Form 10-K identifies these causes of quarter-to-quarter differences in net sales:

- **Seasonality:** First-quarter sales have historically been higher, partly because of holiday demand.
- **Product and service introductions:** Launch timing can affect sales, including sales to indirect distributors as they stock new products and reduce inventories of older ones. Anticipation of a launch by consumers and distributors can also affect sales.
- **Concentration in one product:** A decline in demand for the single product that generates a significant portion of Apple’s net sales could substantially affect a quarter.
- **Unexpected developments:** These include weaker-than-anticipated demand, problems with new introductions, IT or network disruptions, and failures by logistics, component-supply or manufacturing partners.
- **Fiscal-quarter length:** Apple periodically adds a week to its first fiscal quarter; it did so in 2023.

Sources: [Apple 2023 Form 10-K, pp. 4, 15 and 20](AAPL_2023_10K.pdf).

Pfizer attributed the favorable change primarily to **net gains on equity securities in 2023, compared with net losses in 2022, and lower net interest expense**. Higher intangible-asset impairment charges partly offset those benefits. [2023 Form 10-K, p. 40](PFE_2023_10K.pdf#page=48)

| Measure | Effect | What it measures |
|---|---:|---|
| Firmwide allowance for credit losses | **$587 decrease** | The net cumulative adoption adjustment. The same $587 appears as the firmwide decrease in the allowance for loan losses. |
| Consumer loans, excluding credit cards | **$489 decrease** | The adoption adjustment to the allowance for loan losses for this portfolio. |
| Credit card loans | **$100 decrease** | The adoption adjustment to the allowance for loan losses for this portfolio. |
| Wholesale loans | **$2 increase** | The adoption adjustment to the allowance for loan losses for this portfolio. |
| Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) | **$591 decrease** | The net adoption effect on the segment’s allowance for loan losses, driven by residential real estate and credit cards. This is a *business-segment* figure, not the firmwide total. |

- **Exchange gain:** The Firm recognized an initial gain of **$7.990 billion** on May 6, based on the fair value of the Class C shares received. Including second-quarter fair-value changes in the Class C shares and related derivatives, plus dividends, it reported a **$7.9 billion net Visa-related gain**. The gain was included in other income and Corporate results. The initial and net gains are not separate amounts to add together. [Form 10-K, pp. 200, 228](JPM_2024_10K.pdf)
- **Foundation contribution:** The Firm contributed some Class C shares to the JPMorgan Chase Foundation, recording **$1.0 billion of noninterest expense** in the second quarter. It sold the remaining Class C shares in the second and third quarters. Combining the reported net gain and contribution gives **approximately $6.9 billion before tax**, without separately quantifying any later sale effects. [pp. 200, 228](JPM_2024_10K.pdf)
- **Income taxes:** The gain and contribution affected the mix of taxable income and expenses and contributed to the increase in the Firm’s effective tax rate, from **19.6% in 2023 to 22.1% in 2024**. The filing does not isolate a tax amount or rate change attributable to Visa. [p. 62](JPM_2024_10K.pdf)
- **Value-at-risk:** Holding Class C shares elevated average and maximum **Corporate VaR, Other VaR and Total VaR**. Changes in the exposure primarily drove the rise and subsequent decline in daily VaR during the second quarter. Average Total VaR rose from **$43 million to $47 million** in 2024; the **$4 million increase** also reflected purchased credit protection and offsets, so it was not solely attributable to Visa. The filing does not separately quantify Visa’s contribution. [pp. 143–144](JPM_2024_10K.pdf)
